Set when the entry's OWN assembled command needs elevated privilege to run on a STIG'd host that the command text itself never requests (no sudo/su in the template) -- distinct from blast, which rates what the command DOES once it runs, not what it takes to run it. The UI shows a privilege badge next to blast and the evidence exporter records a Requires: line, so the content validation protocol's safety rule (no sudo used during a capture run) can defer the entry correctly instead of silently skipping it (G4(e); gen-sshd-test-config, sshd_config not world-readable on defiant/saratoga, CR-T-34).

entries.notes: H1 correction (Marcus Reed): this entry was wrongly raised to blast yellow at G4(d) on a misreading of -Q as clock-stepping (Caleb Stone's CR-T-34 note read -Q for -q; Eli Cross's ruling and this branch's previous commit both repeated it). chronyd(8) draws a clear line between the two: -q is the mode that actually adjusts the system time and then quits (content-src/raw/rhel8/chronyd.man.txt#L64-L66, identical at rhel10#L64-L66); -Q behaves the same way except for that one adjustment -- it reports the measured offset and, because it skips opening network ports entirely, can run as a non-root user as long as nothing in the config needs elevated access (#L68-L74, identical at rhel10#L68-L74). This toolkit only ever generates -Q. blast restored to green. MCR-SEC-025: chronyd(8) SYNOPSIS is `chronyd [OPTION]... [DIRECTIVE]...` (#L7, identical at rhel10#L7), so configuration directives are OPERANDS accepted after the options, and -Q itself takes no argument (#L68). The directive is a separate word after -Q, never -Q's value. RHEL 7 uses chronyd by default for NTP (chrony package). The legacy ntpd daemon is available as an alternative from the separate ntp package but is not installed or enabled by default on any pinned release (RHEL 7 System Administrator's Guide, ch. 18-19) -- chronyd is the only NTP daemon this toolkit generates commands for.

An ANNOTATED tag (-a) is its own object with a message, tagger identity, and date, and is what git describe and most release tooling expect. Unlike a branch, tags are conventionally never moved once pushed -- retagging the same name to a different commit changes what everyone who already fetched that tag believes it points to.

flags.explain: Create an annotated tag object (message, tagger, date) instead of a lightweight pointer.
Supply the annotated tag's message directly instead of opening an editor.
Delete a local tag.
List existing tags, optionally filtered by a glob pattern.

entries.verify: `git tag -l` lists the tag, and `git show <tag>` shows the expected commit (and, for an annotated tag, the message).
entries.undo: Delete the local tag with `git tag -d <name>` -- if it was already pushed, the remote copy needs its own explicit delete (see git-push's notes on deleting a pushed ref); deleting a tag never touches the commit it pointed at.

entries.intent: See or manage the other repositories this one is configured to fetch from and push to

7.notes: -v (verbose) shows each remote's name alongside its fetch and push URLs, which can legitimately differ. add/remove/rename change the configured remotes; they never touch history or branches by themselves -- fetch/pull/push are the commands that actually move commits.

flags.explain: Show each remote's fetch and push URLs, not just its name.
Register a new remote under a name.
Un-register a remote (does not affect any already-fetched history or remote-tracking branches, beyond no longer updating them).
Change a remote's URL without renaming it.

entries.verify: `git remote -v` lists the expected remote name(s) and URL(s).
entries.undo: Reverse the specific change: `git remote remove <name>` for an added remote, or `git remote add <name> <old-url>` to restore one that was removed -- removing a remote does not delete any commits already fetched from it.

entries.intent: Download a remote's new commits and branches into local remote-tracking branches, without touching the current working branch

7.notes: The safe, non-merging half of pull: it updates origin/<branch> remote-tracking references to match the remote, but never touches the local branch you have checked out or your working tree. Reviewing `git log origin/main..main` or `git diff main origin/main` after a fetch, before merging, is how to see what a pull would bring in before it actually changes anything.

flags.explain: Fetch from every configured remote, not just one.
Remove local remote-tracking branches for branches that no longer exist on the remote.
Also fetch tags that are not already covered by the fetched commits.

entries.verify: `git log origin/<branch>` (or `git branch -r`) shows the expected new remote-tracking history.
entries.undo: Nothing to undo -- fetch only updates remote-tracking references, never the current branch or working tree.

entries.intent: Fetch a remote's new commits and immediately integrate them into the current branch

7.notes: Equivalent to `git fetch` followed by `git merge` (or, with pull.rebase set / --rebase given, `git rebase`) of the remote-tracking branch into the current one -- so everything git-merge's or git-rebase's notes say about conflicts and history rewriting applies here too, just triggered in one step instead of two. `git fetch` first, reviewed, is the safer sequence when the incoming changes are unfamiliar.

flags.explain: Integrate the fetched commits by rebasing the current branch onto them instead of merging.
Refuse to pull unless it can fast-forward -- fails loudly instead of creating a merge commit or rebasing.

entries.verify: `git log` shows the remote's new commits now present on the current branch, with no unexpected merge/rebase result.
entries.undo: The same as the merge or rebase it performed: `git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD` after a merging pull, or the pre-rebase tip from `git reflog` after a rebasing pull.

entries.intent: Upload local commits to a remote, updating its branch to match

7.notes: Normally refuses if the remote branch has commits the local branch does not (someone else pushed first) -- fetch and merge/rebase first rather than forcing past this. --force (or its safer sibling --force-with-lease, which fails if the remote moved since the last fetch instead of blindly overwriting it) REWRITES the remote branch to match local history exactly, discarding whatever commits were only on the remote; on a shared branch this can destroy other people's work with no server-side undo unless the deleted commits happen to still be reachable from someone's reflog or an untouched clone.

flags.explain: Overwrite the remote branch to match local history exactly, discarding remote-only commits with no lease check -- avoid on a shared branch.
Like --force, but refuses if the remote branch has moved since the last fetch, so it cannot blindly discard commits nobody locally has seen yet.
Also push tags that are not already on the remote.
Delete a branch or tag on the remote instead of pushing to it.

entries.verify: The remote's branch (checked with `git log` on a fresh fetch, or the forge's own UI) shows the expected new commits.
entries.undo: A plain push that only added commits is undone with `git push --force` back to the previous remote tip (from local reflog) if nobody else has based work on it yet. A --force push that discarded someone else's commits has no server-side undo -- recovery depends on that history surviving in their local reflog or another clone.

entries.intent: Undo the last commit (or several) while keeping every changed line staged and ready to re-commit -- moves only the branch pointer

7.notes: Of the three reset modes, --soft touches the least: it moves HEAD (and the current branch) to the given commit and leaves both the index and the working tree exactly as they were. This is the direct answer to 'I want to undo the last commit but keep the changes' -- the changes end up staged, as if `git add` had just been run, ready to edit, re-message, or split before committing again.

flags.explain: The commit to move HEAD to, most often HEAD~N (N commits back) or a specific hash.

entries.verify: `git status` shows the undone commit's changes now staged, and `git log` no longer shows that commit.
entries.undo: `git reset --soft <old-tip>` (the hash the branch pointed at before, found in `git reflog`) moves the branch back to where it was.

entries.intent: Undo the last commit (or several) and unstage the changes, leaving them in the working tree as ordinary uncommitted edits

7.notes: --mixed is reset's DEFAULT mode when no mode flag is given. It moves HEAD like --soft, but also resets the index to match the target commit, so the changes show as unstaged modifications in the working tree rather than staged ones. The working tree's actual file content is untouched -- nothing is discarded, only un-staged.

flags.explain: The commit to move HEAD and the index to, most often HEAD~N or a specific hash.

entries.verify: `git status` shows the undone commit's changes as unstaged modifications, and `git log` no longer shows that commit.
entries.undo: `git reset <old-tip>` (the hash from `git reflog`) moves the branch and index back; the working tree was never changed by the mixed reset in the first place.

entries.intent: Undo the last commit (or several) and discard the changes entirely, resetting the working tree to match the target commit exactly

7.notes: The most destructive of the three modes: it moves HEAD, resets the index, AND overwrites every tracked file in the working tree to match the target commit -- any uncommitted staged or unstaged edits at the time of the reset are gone, not just unstaged. It does not touch untracked files. The commit(s) reset away still exist in git's object database until garbage-collected and are usually recoverable via `git reflog` (see the 'I lost a commit' recovery entry), but any uncommitted work that was never part of a commit has no such safety net.

flags.explain: The commit to reset HEAD, the index, and the working tree to, most often HEAD~N or a specific hash.

entries.verify: `git status` reports a clean working tree matching the target commit, and `git log` no longer shows the reset-away commits.
entries.undo: The commits themselves: `git reset --hard <old-tip>` (the hash from `git reflog`) restores the branch. Any UNCOMMITTED changes present at the moment of the hard reset are not in any commit and are not recoverable by git at all.

entries.intent: Undo a commit's changes by creating a new commit that applies the opposite edit, without rewriting any existing history

7.notes: The safe way to undo a commit that has already been pushed and shared: unlike reset, revert never removes or rewrites an existing commit, it only adds a new one on top that cancels the target's changes -- so it is safe to run on a branch other people have already based work on. Reverting a commit whose changes have since been further modified or removed can itself conflict, the same as a merge would, and pauses for resolution.

flags.explain: Apply the revert's changes to the working tree/index but stop before creating the commit, so several reverts can be combined into one.
For reverting a MERGE commit: specify which parent side to treat as the mainline, since a merge commit has more than one.

entries.verify: `git log` shows the new revert commit, and `git diff <target>..HEAD` shows the target commit's changes are gone from the current state.
entries.undo: Revert the revert: `git revert <revert-commit-hash>` re-applies the original change as yet another new commit -- consistent with revert never rewriting history either way.

entries.intent: Binary-search the commit history to find exactly which commit introduced a bug, instead of reading the log by eye

7.notes: After `git bisect start`, mark a known-bad commit (`git bisect bad`) and a known-good one (`git bisect good <commit>`); git checks out a commit halfway between them for testing, and each `git bisect good`/`git bisect bad` verdict halves the remaining range until one commit is left. `git bisect reset` at the end returns to the branch/commit that was checked out before bisect started -- skipping it leaves the repository checked out at whatever commit bisect landed on (a detached HEAD), not back on the original branch.

flags.explain: Begin a bisect session.
Mark the currently checked-out commit (or a named one) as exhibiting the bug.
Mark the currently checked-out commit (or a named one) as not exhibiting the bug.
End the bisect session and return to the branch/commit checked out before it started.
Automate the good/bad marking by running a given script/command against each candidate commit.

entries.verify: Git reports the single first-bad commit at the end of the session, and testing that commit confirms it introduces the bug.
entries.undo: `git bisect reset` at any point ends the session and returns to the original branch -- bisect only checks out commits for testing, it never creates or discards any.

entries.intent: See every position HEAD and each branch have pointed to recently, including commits a reset or rebase moved away from

7.notes: Records a local, per-repository log of where HEAD (and branches) have been, separate from the commit history itself -- this is what makes a hard reset, a rebase, or a branch deletion recoverable: the old tip commit is still listed here (by default for about 90 days) even though it no longer appears in `git log`. Reflog is local only; it is never pushed and a fresh clone has none of it.

flags.explain: Show the reflog for a specific ref (defaults to HEAD).
Prune old reflog entries past their retention window -- reduces how far back recovery can reach.

entries.verify: The listed entries include the operation being investigated (a reset, rebase, checkout, or commit) with the commit hash it moved from/to.
entries.undo: Nothing to undo -- read-only. The recovery it enables (`git reset --hard <hash-from-reflog>`, or `git branch <name> <hash-from-reflog>`) is undone the same way any reset or branch creation is.

entries.intent: Apply one specific commit's changes onto the current branch, without merging or rebasing everything else that commit's branch contains

7.notes: Creates a NEW commit on the current branch with the same changes and message as the named commit, but a different hash and parent -- the source commit is untouched. Used to bring a single fix from one branch to another without pulling in everything else that has happened on the source branch. Like a merge, a cherry-pick that conflicts with the current branch's content stops with conflict markers and waits for resolution.

flags.explain: Apply the changes to the working tree/index but stop before creating the commit, e.g. to cherry-pick several commits into one.
Back out of a cherry-pick that stopped on conflicts, restoring the pre-cherry-pick state.
Append a line to the new commit's message recording which original commit it was cherry-picked from.

entries.verify: `git log` shows the new commit with the expected changes, and `git diff <source-commit> HEAD` (for that file/path) shows the same content landed.
entries.undo: If not yet pushed: `git reset --hard <old-tip>` (from `git reflog`) removes the cherry-picked commit -- the original source commit is never affected either way.

entries.intent: Recovery scenario: 'I committed to the wrong branch' -- move a commit that was just made on the wrong branch onto the right one

7.command: git log -1  # note the hash, then: git checkout right-branch && git cherry-pick <hash> && git checkout wrong-branch && git reset --hard HEAD~1
7.notes: The commit itself is not damaged -- it exists as an object regardless of which branch pointed at it. The fix is additive-then-subtractive: cherry-pick the commit onto the branch it belongs on (a new commit object, same content), THEN remove it from the wrong branch with reset. Doing the cherry-pick BEFORE the reset means the commit is safely copied before anything is removed, so an interruption partway through never leaves the work existing nowhere. If the wrong-branch commit was already pushed, treat removing it there the same as any other push --force: only safe if nobody else has already fetched it.

entries.verify: `git log` on the correct branch shows the commit, and `git log` on the originally-wrong branch no longer shows it.
entries.undo: If interrupted after the cherry-pick but before the reset, the commit now simply exists on both branches -- re-running just the reset half finishes the cleanup; nothing is lost either way since the cherry-pick step never removes anything.

entries.intent: Recovery scenario: 'I lost a commit' -- a hard reset, a rebase, or a deleted branch removed a commit from every branch's visible history

7.command: git reflog  # find the commit's hash, then: git branch recovered-work <hash>
7.notes: A commit that no longer appears in `git log` on any branch is not necessarily gone: as long as it has not been garbage-collected (git's default grace period is long, on the order of weeks, unless someone has run `git gc --prune=now`), it is still a real object in the repository, and `git reflog` almost always still has a line recording the moment HEAD pointed at it. Once the hash is found there, `git branch <new-name> <hash>` recreates a branch pointing at it, or `git cherry-pick <hash>` replays just that commit onto the current branch -- either way the 'lost' commit was never actually deleted, only unreferenced.

entries.verify: `git log <new-branch-or-hash>` shows the recovered commit and its content matches what was expected to be lost.
entries.undo: Nothing further to undo -- this recovery only reads the reflog and creates a new reference; it does not remove anything.
